title: Missing type for PEP695 `TypeAliasType` vs `TypeAlias` when using `TypeAdapter`
issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [X] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

There seems to be a difference between the type that is returned from TypeAdapter when used on a PEP695 `TypeAliasType` compared to when it is used on a `TypeAlias`. See example below. When `TypeAdapter` is used on a `TypeAlias`, the correct type is shown. However, when the `TypeAliasType` is used, the type is shown as `TypeAliasType`. This causes the type-checker to see red. 

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import TypeAlias, reveal_type

from pydantic import TypeAdapter

my_type_alias: TypeAlias = list[dict[str, list[int]]]
x: my_type_alias = [{"a": [1, 2, 3]}]

res = TypeAdapter(type=my_type_alias).validate_python(x)
reveal_type(res)  # type of res is "list[dict[str, list[int]]]"


type my_type = list[dict[str, list[int]]]
x: my_type = [{"a": [1, 2, 3]}]

res = TypeAdapter(type=my_type).validate_python(x)
reveal_type(res)  # type of res is "TypeAliasType"
```


### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
pydantic version: 2.6.3
        pydantic-core version: 2.16.3
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=true
                 install path: /usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages/pydantic
               python version: 3.12.2 (main, Feb 13 2024, 09:17:46) [GCC 12.2.0]
                     platform: Linux-5.15.133.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.36
             related packages: pyright-1.1.352 pyright-1.1.353 typing_extensions-4.10.0 pydantic-extra-types-2.6.0 fastapi-0.110.0 pydantic-settings-2.2.1
                       commit: unknown
```

-assert_type(ta2, TypeAdapter[int])  # type: ignore[assert-type]  # pyright: ignore[reportAssertTypeFailure]
+assert_type(ta2, TypeAdapter[int])

title: Some Field attributes lost in JSON schema when using RootModel

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the core issue the same way: they copy `examples` (made JSON-able) and `deprecated` from the RootModel's `root` FieldInfo into the model-level schema. They also both keep `model_config['title']` ahead of the field title. The deciding difference is title handling. Patch A falls back to `cls.__pydantic_fields__['root'].title` whenever no title has been set, but `FieldInfo.title` can be filled in by a `field_title_generator`, either from config or on the Field. With such a generator, Patch A would rename the model schema to the generated field title (e.g. 'ROOT') instead of the class name, which is a regression for users who set `field_title_generator`. Patch B guards against this by only using an explicitly set title (`_attributes_set.get('title')`), and it adds a test for exactly this case covering both config-level and field-level generators. Patch B also places the explicit root title ahead of `model_title_generator`, which fits the issue's complaint that the field title is overwritten. Patch B also handles `deprecated=''` (an empty message), consolidates the RootModel detection into a single `root_field` variable reused for description, examples, deprecated and `json_schema_extra`, and avoids repeated `issubclass` checks. Its tests are broader and would fail before the change: a deprecation message, serialization mode, a generic `RootModel[Annotated[...]]`, a nested RootModel in `$defs`, config precedence, and the title-generator case. Patch A's tests cover the basic cases but miss the title-generator interaction its own change breaks. B is more correct and better tested.

### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

When declaring a RootModel and adding a `Field` annotation to the `root` property that includes `examples`, those `examples` are not part of the generated JSON schema. This also applies to the `deprecated` attribute. The `title` attribute is also not applied or it is overwritten by the class name of the root model class. 

Most other attributes, such as `pattern` or `description` are exposed as expected. Furthermore, placing `examples` in `json_schema_extra` also works as expected.

from typing import Annotated

class Foo(RootModel):
    root: Annotated[str, Field(examples=["foo", "bar"], deprecated=True)]

title: ValidationError for NamedTuple attributes does not include the attribute name when using `from_attributes=True`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the reported issue: when a NamedTuple instance is validated (including via from_attributes), errors are located by field name instead of index. Each adds a test reproducing the issue's scenario.

Patch B is a small, targeted change. It adds an `item_loc` hook on `PositionalArgs`, which returns the field name when the Python input is a namedtuple instance (it has `_fields` and is not an exact tuple). The arguments validator then uses that name, along with the target parameter's lookup path, so aliases and loc_by_alias match the dict-input behavior. Plain tuples keep index locations. Its tests cover:
- the exact issue reproduction,
- parity with dict input,
- plain tuples still using indices,
- collections.namedtuple inputs with different field names, which are located by the target field name,
- the alias case.

One quirk is that extra items from a namedtuple input are reported under the input's own field names. This is minor.

Patch A replaces the whole 'call'/'arguments' implementation for NamedTuple with a new 'named-tuple' core schema. That includes a new Rust validator and serializer, a new error type, JSON schema generation, and docs changes. This is a large redesign that changes user-visible behavior well beyond the issue:
- `unexpected_positional_argument` becomes `too_long`.
- `unexpected_keyword_argument` becomes `extra_forbidden`.
- `arguments_type` becomes `named_tuple_type`.
- The core schema shape changes, breaking user `__get_pydantic_core_schema__` hooks that touch `arguments_schema`; the patch had to rewrite `test_namedtuple_modify_schema`.
- The JSON schema produced in that customization scenario changes.
- Serialization semantics change.

It also deletes the existing test file and recreates it elsewhere, with existing expectations rewritten to the new error types. The underlying fix is sound, but the churn carries substantial regression and compatibility risk and obscures the fix itself.

Given comparable correctness on the issue and adequate tests on both sides, Patch B's minimal, convention-consistent change is the better fix.

title: Add `FastMCP` and MCP's `python-sdk` to third-party tests

judge.reasoning:
Both patches add `test-mcp-python-sdk` and `test-fastmcp` jobs and wire them into `create-issue-on-failure`, which is what the issue asks for. The difference is in how well the new jobs would actually run.

Patch A's new jobs look tuned to each project's real CI setup:
- It uses the canonical `PrefectHQ/fastmcp` repo.
- It sets `MCP_EXAMPLES_SMOKE=0` so the MCP SDK suite skips smoke tests that spawn stdio and uvicorn subprocesses.
- It unsets the workflow-level `FORCE_COLOR`, which would otherwise make Rich emit ANSI codes and break FastMCP's CLI output assertions.
- It runs FastMCP's unit-test configuration: `--inline-snapshot=disable`, a timeout, and excludes the integration, client_process, subprocess_heavy and conformance markers.
- It covers Python 3.14 for the SDK.
- Its install pattern (uninstall pydantic, then `pip install -e ./pydantic-latest`) matches the existing jobs.

Patch B is simpler but more likely to fail for reasons that have nothing to do with pydantic:
- It runs the full MCP SDK suite with plain `pytest`, including subprocess smoke tests.
- It leaves `FORCE_COLOR` set, so FastMCP's CLI tests are likely to break.
- It omits the inline-snapshot and timeout settings.
- It relies on the `jlowin/fastmcp` redirect.
- It also editable-installs `./pydantic-latest/pydantic-core`, which forces a Rust build and differs from the other jobs.

Patch A has a real downside: substantial unrelated churn. It changes the Beanie, ODMantic, Polar, Dify, Django Ninja and FastDepends jobs. The ODMantic command now passes `tests` twice, and the Dify test invocation is changed. These look like fixes for broken jobs, but they add some risk and are out of scope.

Neither patch adds tests, as expected for CI-only changes. On correctness of the requested jobs, A is meaningfully stronger, and that outweighs the churn.

title: Preserve `NamedTuple` class during validation

judge.reasoning:
Patch A fixes the root cause with a small change in `CallValidator`. When the call target is a class and a smart union is tracking exactness, an input that is an exact instance of that class is marked `Exact`. Any other input is capped at `Strict`. As a result, `B(x=1)` validated against `A | B` stays a `B`, in both lax and strict config. Non-instance inputs still pick left-to-right, a single-type field still converts `B` to `A`, and instance fields are still revalidated (`B('1')` becomes `B(1)`). Its tests cover these cases in pydantic-core and in pydantic for both `typing.NamedTuple` and `collections.namedtuple`, and the core assertions would fail before the change. Existing behaviour outside smart unions is left alone.

Patch B also fixes the union case: its new validator floors non-instance inputs to `Strict` and leaves exact instances untouched. To get there, it replaces the whole namedtuple implementation with a new `named-tuple` core schema, validator, serializer and error type. That carries many user-visible behaviour changes beyond the issue:
- Error types and locations change (`too_long` instead of `unexpected_positional_argument`, `extra_forbidden` instead of `unexpected_keyword_argument`).
- The `arguments_type` docs are rewritten.
- JSON schema output changes (the existing modify-schema test was rewritten, and its expected object schema became an array schema).
- The `pydantic_js_prefer_positional_arguments` metadata hook no longer applies.
- Serialization and union serialization are now handled by new code.
- The existing test file is deleted and recreated with changed expectations.

This broad redesign adds substantial regression and compatibility risk and obscures the actual fix. Both patches resolve the issue, but A does so with far less risk and with focused tests.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

This is what I'm observing:

```Python
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B


c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)

# expected: a_or_b=B(x=1)
# prints: a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

This short-circuits on type arguments in the union in order in the `smart` mode of unions (`left_to_right` I assume makes no difference, the problem lies in exactness).
If we reverse it, the output will show `B` because `B` was first that structurally matched.

It works this way in strict mode too.
This resembles `left_to_right` more than `smart` mode of the union schema.

Conceptually, Pydantic looks for ways to match namedtuple as a structural type, whereas the nominal bit was missed.

This applies to old-fashion named tuples as well:
```py
from collections import namedtuple

import pydantic

A = namedtuple('A', 'x')
B = namedtuple('B', 'x')

class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    a_or_b: A | B

c = C(a_or_b=B(x=1))
print(c)  # a_or_b=A(x=1)
```

We would want to convert between uniform namedtuples in non-strict mode -- sure:

```py
import pydantic
from typing import NamedTuple


class A(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class B(NamedTuple):
    x: int


class C(pydantic.BaseModel):
    only_a: A


c = C(only_a=B(x=1))
print(c)  # only_a=A(x=1)
```

but I'm not so sure we want the union schema to miss the nominal type of the input. If we can preserve the original type, my instinct is that we'd want to keep it. Esp. since we don't observe this behavior with dataclasses (namedtuples are of quite different nature, though).

The current behavior can be interpreted as a feature, not a bug -- feel free to relabel this as a feature request if you do think that's true.

## In short

I'm proposing a feature to, in validation, validate every namedtuple input against its targeted namedtuple class (so, `return_schema` -- seems like `return_schema` isn't used by namedtuple schemas yet) **before** proceeding with the call validator logic and deconstructing it as a collection of arguments and trying a call to the namedtuple constructor. It would be based on a new `idempotent` flag in `CallValidator` -- if a function call is idempotent, the validation should start from the return validator -- if that doesn't pass, only then try to call. As a result, nominal types wouldn't be swapped in unions of namedtuples in smart union mode.

Do you guys think this is worth adding to pydantic, or too much hassle for an edge case?
Thanks!

PS One more thing. This relies on the assumption that instance checks guarantees type safety of the object's state.

If the namedtuple instance contains unsound data, its internals wouldn't be re-validated and fixed up in place as it happens right now. In this sense, the change could be breaking. 

The same that would happen here already happens for dataclasses in Pydantic:

```py
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic import BaseModel


@dataclass
class Foo:
    x: int


malformed = Foo(x="1")

class Model(BaseModel):
    foo: Foo

print(Model(foo=malformed))
```

If someone has an unsure instance of a namedtuple, they would need to re-validate it through type adapter, perhaps.
Or just use models directly on raw data -- for 99.999% of people this won't happen.

title: mypy `[arg-type]`-error when passing in type that can be converted to `RootModel`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make essentially the same core change in `pydantic/mypy.py`. They register `_RootModelMetaclass` with the metaclass hook so the dataclass_transform spec is reset. They also let the plugin generate `__init__` for `RootModel` itself instead of keeping its explicit typed `__init__`. This fixes the root cause: with the plugin and `init_typed` unset, `RootModel[float]('1.0')` is accepted, just as `BaseModel` fields are. The only code difference is `self._cls.info.fullname` (A) versus `self._cls.fullname` (B). Both resolve to the same value, so correctness is equal. A also updates the metaclass-callback docstring to mention the RootModel metaclass, a small craft point.

The real difference is test coverage. B tests only the type-alias and subclass forms, and only in `root_models.py` with and without the plugin. A tests three forms: the alias, direct `RootModel[float]('1.0')` (the issue's form), and a subclass. It adds a `BaseModel` comparison case to show parity. It also adds cases to `plugin_fail.py` that run under the `init_typed=True` (strict) configs. There the expected errors appear for both `BaseModel` and `RootModel`, confirming that RootModel now follows the plugin's `init_typed` setting rather than always being typed. That covers the other half of the behavior change, which B leaves untested. A's 5 'removed' test lines are just the updated import lines. A is the stronger patch because of its broader and more meaningful tests.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

The below example code (named `foo.py`) passes when running `python foo.py` as the input `"1.0"`-string gets converted to `float`. However, running `mypy foo.py` (with or without `--strict`) gives the following error:
```bash
foo.py:11: error: Argument 1 to "RootModel" has incompatible type "str"; expected "float"  [arg-type]
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
```
I would expect the `BaseModel`-fields and the `RootModel`-field to behave the same in this case. That is, if the value can be converted – either via a custom made validator or through the conversion table – then `mypy` should not raise an error. 

### Example Code

```Python
import pydantic


class Foo(pydantic.BaseModel):
    f: float


RFoo = pydantic.RootModel[float]

f = Foo(f="1.0")
rf = RFoo("1.0")

assert isinstance(f.f, float)
assert isinstance(rf.root, float)
assert f.f == rf.root
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text
pydantic version: 2.12.5
        pydantic-core version: 2.41.5

```

title: Decimal JSON schema pattern rejects pydantic's own scientific notation serialization output (v2.12 regression)

judge.reasoning: Patch A fixes the root cause the issue names. It adds an optional `[eE][+-]?\d+` exponent to every generated Decimal pattern. It also tightens the leading negative lookahead so strings like 'e5' or '.e5' are still rejected. In the constrained branches it adds an exponent alternative that bounds only the mantissa digits, and a comment documents that the exponent-dependent digit count cannot be expressed in a regex. This follows the first fix the issue suggests, keeps the existing feature (the patterns introduced in 2.12), and stays close to the surrounding code style. Its tests are targeted and meaningful, and they would fail on the old pattern: they serialize real values (1E-7, 0E-10, -1.23E+10, constrained cases) via `model_dump_json`/`dump_json`, check the output with `re.fullmatch` against both the validation and serialization schemas, round-trip the value, and confirm malformed exponent strings are rejected. Patch B instead drops the pattern from the default schema entirely. That makes the reported symptom disappear, but it does so by reverting the feature for everyone, which is a significant behavior change. It moves the logic into new public hooks (`get_decimal_pattern`, `build_decimal_pattern`) backed by a large, intricate regex builder that handles serialization-exact patterns, exponent ranges and inf/nan. Most of that machinery is opt-in, so the default-path fix is effectively 'remove the pattern'. The change adds considerable code and risk, and it includes unrelated churn (moving `_HashableJsonValue`). Its docs are confusing: two contradictory 'version-changed' blocks, one saying the pattern is included and one saying it no longer is. B's tests are extensive, but they mostly exercise the new opt-in builder rather than the default behavior the issue reports. On correctness and scope, A resolves the issue directly with low risk, while B is a broad redesign that masks the issue by default and adds complexity.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

**`model_json_schema(mode="serialization")` pattern for `Decimal` breaks on scientific notation**

The serialization schema for `Decimal` fields generates a regex that rejects values that `model_dump_json()` itself produces.

Specifically: `pydantic-core`'s serializer calls `str()` on `Decimal` objects, which outputs scientific notation for small/large values. E.g. `Decimal('0.0000001')` becomes `"1E-7"`. But the pattern added in #11987 (`^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\d*\.?\d*$`) has no `[eE]` component, so it'll never match those strings.

As a result, any downstream consumer validating `model_dump_json()` output against `model_json_schema()`, such as OpenAPI validators and codegen + validation tools like Orval + Zod, will intermittently reject perfectly valid serialized values. Intermittent because only certain `Decimal` values trigger scientific notation.

**v2.11**:
```json
{"anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]}
```

**v2.12**:
```json
{"anyOf": [{"pattern": "^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\\d*\\.?\\d*$", "type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}]}
```

Two possible fixes:
- Append `(?:[eE][+-]?\d+)?` to the pattern in serialization mode
- Normalize `Decimal` to fixed-point during serialization before it ever hits the schema

### Example Code

```Python
import json
import re
from decimal import Decimal
from pydantic import BaseModel

class MyModel(BaseModel):
    value: Decimal | None

schema = MyModel.model_json_schema(mode="serialization")
pattern = next(
    v for v in schema["properties"]["value"]["anyOf"] if v.get("type") == "string"
)["pattern"]
regex = re.compile(pattern)

# pydantic serializes this as "1E-7" which fails its own schema's pattern
m = MyModel(value=Decimal("0.0000001"))
serialized = json.loads(m.model_dump_json())["value"]

print(f"Pattern: {pattern}")
print(f"Serialized: {serialized!r}")
print(f"Matches: {bool(regex.match(serialized))}")
# Pattern: ^(?!^[-+.]*$)[+-]?0*\d*\.?\d*$
# Serialized: '1E-7'
# Matches: False
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```Text

pydantic-core version: 2.41.5
pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
python version: 3.12.11 | packaged by conda-forge | (main, Jun  4 2025, 14:38:53) [Clang 18.1.8 ]
platform: macOS-26.2-arm64-arm-64bit
related packages: pyright-1.1.408 pydantic-extra-types-2.10.5 typing_extensions-4.15.0 fastapi-0.123.0 pydantic-settings-2.10.1
commit: unknown
```

+# Decimal JSON Schema pattern utilities.
+# Note: while we could use `\d` to represent digits (`Decimal` objects allow Unicode decimal digits), we use [0-9] instead:
+# - to reduce complexity (`\d` expands to a large set, and with `max_digits`/`decimal_places` constraints set, it can blow
+#   the compile limit on some engines).
+# - [0-9] is a portable pattern (e.g. `\d` is equivalent to `[0-9]` in ECMA (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Regular_expressions/Character_class_escape#d)
+#   while it allows any Unicode decimal digit in Python.
+
+
+def _repeat(atom: str, min_count: int, max_count: int) -> str:
+    """Build a regex repetition of `atom` between `min_count` and `max_count` times (inclusive), using the shortest quantifier."""
+    if min_count > max_count or max_count == 0:
+        return ''
+    if min_count == max_count:
+        return atom if min_count == 1 else f'{atom}{{{min_count}}}'
+    if (min_count, max_count) == (0, 1):
+        return f'{atom}?'
+    return f'{atom}{{{min_count},{max_count}}}'
+
+
+def _int_range_pattern(max_value: int) -> str:
+    """Build a regex matching the integers between 1 and `max_value` (inclusive), without leading zeros."""
+    digits = str(max_value)
+    length = len(digits)
+    alts: list[str] = [f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", k - 1, k - 1)}' for k in range(1, length)]
+    for i, char in enumerate(digits):
+        d = int(char)
+        low = 1 if i == 0 else 0
+        high = d if i == length - 1 else d - 1
+        if high >= low:
+            char_class = str(low) if low == high else f'[{low}-{high}]'
+            alts.append(f'{digits[:i]}{char_class}{_repeat("[0-9]", length - i - 1, length - i - 1)}')
+    return alts[0] if len(alts) == 1 else f'(?:{"|".join(alts)})'
+
+
+def _decimal_validation_pattern(max_digits: int | None, decimal_places: int | None, allow_inf_nan: bool) -> str:
+    """Build the decimal pattern for the `'validation'` mode."""
+
+    number = r'(?:[0-9]+\.?[0-9]*|\.[0-9]+)'  # e.g. 1, 1., .5
+    exponent = r'[eE][+-]?[0-9]+'  # e.g. e5, E5, e-7
+    # e.g. Infinity, inf, NaN, sNaN, NaN123 (case-insensitive). Spelled out explicitly, as inline flags
+    # aren't supported by all regular expression engines:
+    non_finite = r'|[iI][nN][fF](?:[iI][nN][iI][tT][yY])?|[sS]?[nN][aA][nN][0-9]*' if allow_inf_nan else ''
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        return rf'^[+-]?(?:{number}(?:{exponent})?{non_finite})$'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:
+        # If `decimal_places > max_digits`, no whole digits are allowed and `max_digits` bounds the decimal places:
+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)
+        places = min(max_digits, decimal_places)
+        int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, whole)}' if whole else '0+'
+        opt_int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, whole)}'
+        opt_frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, places)}0*'
+        frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+        alts += [f'{int_part}(?:{opt_frac_part})?', f'{opt_int_part}{frac_part}']
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        int_part = f'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}' if max_digits else '0+'
+        alts.append(rf'{int_part}(?:\.0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            rf'0*{_repeat("[0-9]", whole, whole)}\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits - whole)}0*'
+            for whole in range(max_digits)
+        ] or [r'0*\.0+']
+    else:
+        assert decimal_places is not None
+        opt_frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, decimal_places)}0*'
+        frac_part = rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, decimal_places)}0*' if decimal_places else r'\.0+'
+        alts += [f'[0-9]+(?:{opt_frac_part})?', f'[0-9]*{frac_part}']
+
+    alts.append(f'{number}{exponent}')
+    return rf'^[+-]?(?:{"|".join(alts)}{non_finite})$'

+def _decimal_serialization_pattern(max_digits: int | None, decimal_places: int | None, allow_inf_nan: bool) -> str:
+    """Build the decimal pattern for the `'serialization'` mode.
+
+    Decimals are serialized using `str()`, producing either:
+
+    - The plain notation (`'123.45'`), when the exponent is lower than or equal to 0 and the adjusted
+      exponent is greater than or equal to -6.
+    - The scientific notation otherwise (`'1E+3'`, `'1.5E-7'`, `'0E-10'`), with a single digit before
+      the optional decimal point and an always signed exponent.
+
+    Trailing zeros of the decimal part are preserved by `str()`, but aren't counted by the validation logic.
+    """
+
+    def frac_part(places: int) -> str:
+        return rf'\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, places)}0*' if places else r'\.0+'
+
+    alts: list[str] = []
+
+    # Plain notation:
+    if max_digits is not None and decimal_places is not None:
+        whole = max(0, max_digits - decimal_places)
+        places = min(max_digits, decimal_places)
+        int_part = f'(?:0|[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", 0, whole - 1)})' if whole else '0'
+        alts.append(f'{int_part}(?:{frac_part(places)})?')
+    elif max_digits is not None:
+        # The whole part and decimal part must have at most `max_digits` digits in total,
+        # so we enumerate the possible widths of the whole part:
+        alts.append(rf'0(?:\.{_repeat("[0-9]", 1, max_digits)}0*)?')
+        alts += [
+            f'[1-9]{_repeat("[0-9]", whole - 1, whole - 1)}(?:{frac_part(max_digits - whole)})?'
+            for whole in range(1, max_digits + 1)
+        ]
+    elif decimal_places is not None:
+        alts.append(f'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:{frac_part(decimal_places)})?')
+    else:
+        alts.append(r'(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:\.[0-9]+)?')
+
+    # Zero with an exponent (e.g. `'0E-10'`), which normalizes to zero and thus satisfies any constraint:
+    alts.append(r'0E[+-][1-9][0-9]*')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a positive exponent `k` (e.g. `'1.5E+3'`): the value has `k + 1` whole digits
+    # and no decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_exponent = max_digits - (decimal_places or 0) - 1
+        if max_exponent >= 1:
+            alts.append(rf'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E\+{_int_range_pattern(max_exponent)}')
+
+    # Scientific notation with a negative exponent `k` (`k >= 7`, e.g. `'1.5E-7'`): the value has no whole digits,
+    # and `k` + (the number of significant decimal digits of the coefficient) decimal places:
+    if max_digits is None and decimal_places is None:
+        alts.append(r'[1-9](?:\.[0-9]+)?E-[1-9][0-9]*')
+    else:
+        max_places = min(c for c in (max_digits, decimal_places) if c is not None)
+        alts += [f'[1-9](?:{frac_part(max_places - k)})?E-{k}' for k in range(7, max_places + 1)]
+
+    if allow_inf_nan:
+        # `str()` produces `'Infinity'`, `'NaN'` and `'sNaN'` (with an optional payload):
+        alts += ['Infinity', 's?NaN[0-9]*']
+
+    return rf'^-?(?:{"|".join(alts)})$'

title: 'fraction_validator' raises unhandled 'ZeroDivisionError' for zero-denominator string input instead of 'ValidationError'

judge.reasoning:
Both patches stop `Fraction('6/0')` from escaping as a raw `ZeroDivisionError`. Patch B does it at the root cause the issue names: it adds `ZeroDivisionError` to the except tuple in `fraction_validator`, exactly as proposed. It also adds targeted tests for `'6/0'`, `'0/0'` and `'-1/0'`. These cover `validate_python`, `validate_json` and `validate_strings` in both strict and lax mode, and check the exact error type, message and input. All of them would fail before the change and pass after. B also updates the two existing tests that had encoded the buggy `ZeroDivisionError` behavior.

Patch A rewrites fraction handling as a new Rust core validator and serializer. It adds a new core schema type and new error types, and moves `get_fraction_type`. It changes `fraction_as_int` semantics and changes the JSON schema output in validation mode (now an `anyOf` with a number branch). It also deletes several existing tests: the `BaseModel`-based fraction tests in `tests/test_types.py` and the `Model` usage in `test_fraction.py`. Its error mapping does cover `ZeroDivisionError`, and it also folds in `OverflowError` and `TypeError`. However, the redesign adds a lot of risk, changes public behavior well beyond the issue, and removes coverage. That makes the actual fix hard to isolate and review.

Under the criteria, correctness on the reported issue is roughly equal, Patch B's tests are clean and targeted, and Patch A's scope adds meaningful risk and obscures the fix. Patch B is the better fix.

### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

**Bug description**

The `fraction_validator` in `pydantic/_internal/_validators.py` only catches `ValueError` when constructing a `fractions.Fraction` from user input. However, Python's standard `fractions.Fraction` raises `ZeroDivisionError` when the denominator is zero (e.g., the string `"6/0"`). Because this exception is not caught, it bubbles up as a raw Python exception instead of being converted into a `ValidationError`, violating Pydantic's contract that all invalid user input should result in a `ValidationError`.

This was discovered during fuzzing of `TypeAdapter.validate_strings()` with the Atheris fuzzer.

**Expected behavior**

A `pydantic.ValidationError` should be raised with a message indicating that the input is not a valid fraction.

**Actual behavior**

```python
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../pydantic/_internal/_validators.py", line 253, in fraction_validator
    return Fraction(input_value)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File ".../fractions.py", line 281, in __new__
    raise ZeroDivisionError('Fraction(%s, 0)' % numerator)
ZeroDivisionError: Fraction(6, 0)
```

**Root cause**

In `pydantic/_internal/_validators.py`, line 247-254:

```python
def fraction_validator(input_value: Any, /) -> Fraction:
    if isinstance(input_value, Fraction):
        return input_value

    try:
        return Fraction(input_value)
    except ValueError:
        raise PydanticCustomError('fraction_parsing', 'Input is not a valid fraction')
```

The `except` clause only catches `ValueError`, but `Fraction("6/0")` raises `ZeroDivisionError`.

**Proposed fix**

Add `ZeroDivisionError` to the exception tuple:

```diff
--- a/pydantic/_internal/_validators.py
+++ b/pydantic/_internal/_validators.py
@@ -250,7 +250,7 @@ def fraction_validator(input_value: Any, /) -> Fraction:
 
     try:
         return Fraction(input_value)
-    except ValueError:
+    except (ValueError, ZeroDivisionError):
         raise PydanticCustomError('fraction_parsing', 'Input is not a valid fraction')
```

This is consistent with how other validators in the same file handle exceptions from standard library constructors (e.g., `decimal_validator`, `uuid_validator`, `ip_*_validators`).

The bug exists and not fixed in 'main' branch as well.

### Example Code

```Python
from pydantic import TypeAdapter
import fractions

adapter = TypeAdapter(fractions.Fraction)

# This should raise ValidationError, but raises ZeroDivisionError
adapter.validate_strings("6/0")
```

title: `PrivateAttr(default_factory=...)`: `takes_validated_data_argument` re-runs `inspect.signature` on every instantiation (uncached) → CPU + cyclic-GC memory churn

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause: they cache the `takes_validated_data_argument` result on `ModelPrivateAttr` and pass it into `resolve_default_value`, so each private-attr instantiation stops calling `inspect.signature` twice. Patch A is better on correctness, tests and risk.

**Correctness.**
- Patch A keys its cache on the factory's identity, `(default_factory, takes_data)`, so reassigning `default_factory` correctly invalidates it. Patch B caches with a `_Unset` sentinel and never invalidates, so reassigning the factory leaves a stale flag.
- Patch A only computes the flag when `call_default_factory` is true. It also keeps `resolve_default_value`'s fallback, so the new parameter is optional and backward compatible.
- Patch B now eagerly evaluates `self.default_factory_takes_validated_data` in `FieldInfo.get_default` even when `call_default_factory=False`. `FieldInfo`'s property is still uncached, so this adds signature inspections on paths that never needed one. That is a small regression for regular fields.
- Patch B also makes `resolve_default_value` keyword-only with a new required argument. That is a breaking signature change that risks any other caller.
- Patch A also caches on `FieldInfo`, which speeds up `model_construct`. It uses `getattr` with a default for robustness.

**Tests.**
- Patch A adds call-counting regression tests that would fail before the fix and pass after. They cover private attrs with and without a validated-data factory, cache invalidation on reassignment, `model_construct`, and an unchanged repr.
- Patch B adds no test that checks the caching at all. Its test changes are repr tests and a mechanical rewrite of the existing `resolve_default_value` tests to the new signature.

**Scope and craft.**
- Patch B changes `ModelPrivateAttr`'s repr (it drops `default=PydanticUndefined`) and edits a docstring, both unrelated to the issue. The repr change is a user-visible behavior change.
- Patch A adds a `__repr_args__` only to keep the existing repr unchanged now that a cache slot exists.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

For a **private attribute** with a `default_factory`, **every model instantiation** re-derives whether the factory takes the validated data by calling `takes_validated_data_argument(default_factory=...)`, which runs `inspect.signature()` on the factory (`pydantic/_internal/_fields.py:694`) — **not cached**, even though it's a pure function of the factory object. It runs **twice per instantiation**, from two separate sites in `init_private_attributes()` (`pydantic/_internal/_model_construction.py:377`): once via the `ModelPrivateAttr.default_factory_takes_validated_data` property, and once via `get_default()` → `resolve_default_value()` (`_fields.py:718`). Both are uncached.


Regular `Field(default_factory=...)` is **not** affected — it computes this once at schema-build time via `FieldInfo.default_factory_takes_validated_data` and bakes it into the core validator. Only the `PrivateAttr` path recomputes per instance.

For a factory whose `inspect.signature()` succeeds via CPython's `inspect._signature_fromstr` (`list`, `tuple`, `set`, `threading.Lock`, …), that call does `sys.modules.copy()` and builds closures that capture the copy — **reference cycles** the plain refcounter can't free, only the cyclic GC can. Instantiating such a model at a high rate in a long-running process accumulates this garbage faster than the collector reclaims it (and pymalloc keeps the freed arenas), so RSS climbs steadily.

Concretely: [Sculptor](https://github.com/imbue-ai/sculptor) has a `BaseModel` with `_wait_lock: Lock = PrivateAttr(default_factory=Lock)` that is instantiated constantly. It was harmless on Python ≤3.12 — there `inspect.signature(Lock)` raises `ValueError: no signature found`, so pydantic falls back cheaply — but began leaking **multi-GB of RSS** on 3.13+, because CPython 3.13 gave `threading.Lock` an inferrable signature and flipped every instantiation onto the `_signature_fromstr` path. We mitigated it by memoizing this check: [imbue-ai/sculptor#205](https://github.com/imbue-ai/sculptor/pull/205).

With `default_factory=list` it reproduces on every CPython tested (**3.12.11, 3.13.5, 3.14.6**) and on pydantic **2.13.4 through `main` (2.14.0a1)** — ~52k objects of cycle-only garbage per 1000 instantiations. `list`/`tuple` have always had signatures, so the bug isn't tied to a Python version; the set of *other* builtins that trigger it just grows over time (`set`, `threading.Lock` at 3.13).

### Example Code

```python
import gc
from pydantic import BaseModel, PrivateAttr
from pydantic._internal import _fields

# (1) It's recomputed on every instantiation, uncached:
calls = 0
_orig = _fields.takes_validated_data_argument
def _counting(*args, **kwargs):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return _orig(*args, **kwargs)
_fields.takes_validated_data_argument = _counting

class M(BaseModel):
    _items: list = PrivateAttr(default_factory=list)

M()                       # warm
calls = 0
for _ in range(1000):
    M()
print("takes_validated_data_argument calls:", calls)   # -> 2000

# (2) Each call leaves cycle-only garbage (default_factory=list):
gc.collect(); gc.disable()
before = len(gc.get_objects())
for _ in range(1000):
    M()
after = len(gc.get_objects())
freed = gc.collect(); gc.enable()
print("objects grew:", after - before, "| freed only by cyclic gc:", freed)
# -> objects grew: ~54000 | freed only by cyclic gc: ~52000
```

### Suggested fix

The simplest fix is to memoize `takes_validated_data_argument` (a pure function of the factory, e.g. `functools.cache`) — after the first call per factory, both per-instance calls become cache hits.

Alternatively, do what regular fields do and compute the flag **once** at class-construction time, storing it so both sites can read it. Note this is more than "reuse the property": `ModelPrivateAttr.default_factory_takes_validated_data` (`pydantic/fields.py:1451`) is itself an uncached `@property` that re-runs `inspect.signature` on every access — it's one of the two per-instance calls, so it has to be precomputed too, not just read from `resolve_default_value`.

Happy to open a PR if you'd like.

          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.14.6 (main, Jun 11 2026, 03:55:33) [Clang 22.1.3 ]

```

Also reproduced on `main` (pydantic 2.14.0a1 / pydantic-core 2.47.0) and on CPython 3.12.11 / 3.13.5.

title: "dictionary changed size during iteration" during `model_rebuild`

judge.reasoning:
Patch A fixes the root cause. The race comes from several threads running `model_rebuild()` on the same class at once: one thread mutates the class `__dict__` (delattr/setattr of the schema, validator and serializer) while another iterates `vars(cls)` inside `LazyLocalNamespace.data` during annotation evaluation. A wraps the rebuild body in a global reentrant lock and re-checks `__pydantic_complete__` inside the lock. That serializes rebuilds and ensures only one thread completes the model, so the on-complete hook runs once. The lock is reentrant because a rebuild can trigger a nested rebuild through generic parametrization (`__class_getitem__` → origin `model_rebuild`). It is global rather than per-class, which avoids cross-class deadlocks, and the comments explain both choices. A also stops deleting `MockCoreSchema` instances, closing the window where concurrent readers fall back to the parent's attributes. That removes the sibling `AttributeError` race the issue mentions. Its two tests are well designed. One checks that reentrant nested rebuilds don't deadlock. The other uses events to force a second thread to block on the lock and then return `None` once the first thread completes the model, with the hook called exactly once. That is a deterministic test of the new concurrency contract, not a probabilistic stress test.

Patch B treats the symptoms. It snapshots the namespaces with C-level `dict.copy()` in `LazyLocalNamespace.data` and in `_decorator_infos_for_class`, and it swallows `AttributeError` around `delattr`. That suppresses the two reported exceptions, but concurrent rebuilds still run in parallel and mutate class state under each other. B's own test admits this: it says `model_rebuild()` 'isn't fully thread-safe' and that a validator can temporarily fall back to the `BaseModel` mock. The test then filters the collected errors down to only the two reported messages, so other failures from the same race are hidden. B also relies on `dict.copy()` being effectively atomic under the GIL, which is not guaranteed on free-threaded builds. Finally, it adds `try/except` blocks that hide real concurrent deletes instead of preventing them. B's stress tests are closer to the issue's reproducer, but they are probabilistic and narrowly filtered.

On correctness, which carries the most weight, A addresses the actual unsynchronized-rebuild bug, while B only masks the visible exceptions.

### Example Code

```Python
"""
NOTE: Repro script generated with Claude Fable

Repro: concurrent lazy `model_rebuild()` raises
`RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`.

Setup: a module using `from __future__ import annotations` defines models whose
field types are only defined *later* in the same module. Building such a model's
schema fails during class creation, so pydantic leaves it incomplete (mock
validator) and defers the build to the first instantiation via
`model_rebuild(raise_errors=False)`.

If the first instantiations happen concurrently (e.g. FastAPI's threadpool
serving the first requests after process start), multiple threads enter
`model_rebuild()` for the same class simultaneously. `model_rebuild()` mutates
the class `__dict__` (delattr/setattr of `__pydantic_core_schema__`,
`__pydantic_validator__`, `__pydantic_serializer__`), while
`NsResolver.types_namespace` includes the live `vars(cls)` of that class in the
`LazyLocalNamespace` another thread is iterating during annotation evaluation
(`LazyLocalNamespace.data`). Result:

    RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration

The same race also intermittently produces
    AttributeError: type object 'Box0' has no attribute '__pydantic_core_schema__'
from the delattr block at the top of `model_rebuild()`.

Each round executes the module source into a fresh module (fresh, incomplete
classes -- like a freshly started process) and races threads instantiating the
models. Typically fires within a few dozen rounds (< 1 min).

Run: python pydantic_rebuild_race_repro.py
"""

import sys
import threading
import time
import traceback
import types

import pydantic

print(f"python {sys.version}")
print(f"pydantic {pydantic.VERSION}")

sys.setswitchinterval(1e-5)  # more frequent thread preemption; widens the race window

N_GENERICS = 2  # generic origins shared by all models (parametrizing triggers origin.model_rebuild)
N_LEAVES = 16  # leaf models, defined at the end of the module so everything before stays incomplete
N_MODELS = 4  # top-level models, the ones instantiated by the racing threads
N_METHODS = 60  # dummy methods to enlarge each class __dict__ (the dict iterated during annotation eval)
N_THREADS = 32
ROUNDS = 200
RACE_WINDOW_S = 0.5


def make_module_source() -> str:
    boxes = " | ".join(f"Box{g}[Leaf{l}]" for g in range(N_GENERICS) for l in range(N_LEAVES))
    methods = [f"    def method{m}(self) -> None: ..." for m in range(N_METHODS)]
    lines = ["from __future__ import annotations", "from pydantic import BaseModel", ""]
    # Top-level models come first: all their field types are still undefined here,
    # so their schema build is deferred until first instantiation.
    for i in range(N_MODELS):
        lines += [f"class Model{i}(BaseModel):", f"    items: list[{boxes}] = []", *methods, ""]
    for g in range(N_GENERICS):
        lines += [f"class Box{g}[T](BaseModel):", "    value: T | None = None", "    ref: Leaf0 | None = None", *methods, ""]
    for l in range(N_LEAVES):
        lines += [f"class Leaf{l}(BaseModel):", "    x: int = 0", ""]
    return "\n".join(lines)


MODULE_SOURCE = make_module_source()

errors: list[str] = []
errors_lock = threading.Lock()


def worker(barrier: threading.Barrier, model: type) -> None:
    barrier.wait()
    end = time.monotonic() + RACE_WINDOW_S
    while time.monotonic() < end:
        try:
            model()  # first call hits the mock validator -> lazy model_rebuild()
        except Exception:
            with errors_lock:
                errors.append(traceback.format_exc())


for rnd in range(ROUNDS):
    # Fresh module => fresh incomplete classes, like a freshly started process.
    mod = types.ModuleType(f"repro_generated_{rnd}")
    sys.modules[mod.__name__] = mod
    exec(compile(MODULE_SOURCE, mod.__name__, "exec"), mod.__dict__)
    models = [getattr(mod, f"Model{i}") for i in range(N_MODELS)]
    assert not models[0].__pydantic_complete__

    barrier = threading.Barrier(N_THREADS)
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(barrier, models[i % N_MODELS])) for i in range(N_THREADS)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    hits = [tb for tb in errors if "changed size during iteration" in tb]

title: `to_json`: `timedelta_mode` and `temporal_mode` break documented behavior

judge.reasoning: Patch B fixes the root cause. It adds a separate `timedelta_mode` field to `SerializationConfig` and stops folding the legacy `timedelta_mode` into the unified `temporal_mode`. With that change, `datetime`, `date` and `time` follow `temporal_mode` while `timedelta` follows `timedelta_mode`. When `temporal_mode` is set to `seconds` or `milliseconds` it still takes precedence for timedeltas, which keeps that feature working. The resolution is applied consistently in the `to_json`/`to_jsonable_python` argument path, in the `ser_json_*` config path, in the inferred (Any) serializer for value, serialize and json-key paths, and in `TimeDeltaSerializer`, which now shares a helper. Patch B also adds targeted tests that would fail before the change and pass after it: the issue's exact example, parametrized combinations of the two modes, dict keys, a config-based Any serializer, and a pydantic `BaseModel` with `ser_json_timedelta='float'`. The `.pyi` docs are updated to describe the override. Patch A changes only docstrings and `config.py` text, with no behavior change and no tests. Its new docs also do not describe the reported behavior accurately: they still present `timedelta_mode` as affecting only timedeltas, while in fact `timedelta_mode='float'` with `temporal_mode='iso8601'` still turns datetimes into floats. So Patch A neither fixes the bug nor correctly documents it, and the issue explicitly prefers independent timedelta control. Patch B is clearly better.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`pydantic_core.to_json` (and `to_jsonable_python`) documents `timedelta_mode` and `temporal_mode` as independent parameters governing disjoint type sets:

> - `timedelta_mode`: How to serialize `timedelta` objects, either `'iso8601'` or `'float'`.
> - `temporal_mode`: How to serialize datetime-like objects (`datetime`, `date`, `time`), either `'iso8601'`, `'seconds'`, or `'milliseconds'`.

(This is what both the [API docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/api/pydantic-core/pydantic_core/) and the shipped `_pydantic_core.pyi` type stub say.)

Given that contract, `to_json(..., timedelta_mode="float", temporal_mode="iso8601")` should serialize `datetime`/`date`/`time` as ISO 8601 strings and `timedelta` as a float. Instead, `datetime`/`date`/`time` are **also** coerced to unix-timestamp floats, `timedelta_mode="float"` silently overrides `temporal_mode="iso8601"` for all temporal types.

There is no combination of the two parameters that yields ISO datetimes with float-second timedeltas, even though the documented parameters imply there should be.

**Root cause / regression.** This regressed in [#1743](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-core/pull/1743). Before that PR, `SerializationConfig` had a dedicated `timedelta_mode: TimedeltaMode` field and `to_json` had no `temporal_mode` parameter, so `timedelta_mode` was genuinely independent. #1743 replaced the dedicated field with a single unified `temporal_mode` and retrofitted `timedelta_mode` as a legacy alias that maps into it.

Either the docs/`.pyi` should be corrected to state that `timedelta_mode` is a deprecated alias that affects all temporal types, or (preferably) `timedelta` should retain an independent setting so the documented behavior holds. Personally I have a requirement to be able to set the `timedelta` format independent of the other `datetime` types.

### Example Code

```Python
import datetime

title: Experimental pipeline: `Interval` bounds of zero are silently dropped

judge.reasoning:
The source changes are byte-for-byte identical. Both replace the four truthiness checks in the `Interval` branch of `_apply_constraint` with `is not None`, which fixes the root cause for all four bounds. Correctness and scope are therefore equal, and the decision rests on tests.

Both patches add cases that would fail before the fix and pass after it.

Patch B strengthens the existing parametrized cases:
- `Interval(ge=0, le=10)` now also rejects `-5`.
- `Interval(gt=0.0, lt=10.0)` now also rejects `0.0` and `-5.0`.
- New int-only cases cover `gt=0`, `le=0` and `lt=0`.
This is tidy, since it fixes the weak existing case (which only checked `11` and so never exercised the zero bound) rather than adding a near-duplicate.

Patch A leaves the weak existing case in place but adds broader zero-bound coverage:
- All four bounds on int, matching every row of the issue's table.
- All four bounds individually on float, with the boundary value itself tested as valid or invalid as appropriate (`0.0` for `ge`/`le`, `0.0` rejected for `gt`/`lt`).
- A `Decimal` case with `ge=Decimal('0')`.
B has no `Decimal` zero-bound case and no float `ge`/`le`/`lt` zero cases in isolation.

B is marginally cleaner because it avoids a semi-duplicate case. However, tests outrank craft, and A's coverage across int, float and Decimal is more thorough. That gives A a small edge.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In `pydantic/experimental/pipeline.py`, `_apply_constraint()` handles `annotated_types.Interval` by delegating to the individual comparison constraints, but it tests each bound for **truthiness** rather than `is not None`:

```python
elif isinstance(constraint, annotated_types.Interval):
    if constraint.ge:
        s = _apply_constraint(s, annotated_types.Ge(constraint.ge))
    if constraint.gt:
        s = _apply_constraint(s, annotated_types.Gt(constraint.gt))
    if constraint.le:
        s = _apply_constraint(s, annotated_types.Le(constraint.le))
    if constraint.lt:
        s = _apply_constraint(s, annotated_types.Lt(constraint.lt))
```

Since `0` is falsy, **a bound of exactly zero is skipped and the constraint is silently dropped** - there is no error, validation simply accepts out-of-range values. `Interval(ge=0, le=10)` happily accepts `-5`.

All four bounds are affected. Observed on 2.12.5:

| constraint | input | expected | actual |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Interval(ge=0, le=10)` | `-5` | ValidationError | **accepted** |
| `Interval(ge=0, le=10)` | `20` | ValidationError | ValidationError (`le=10` works) |
| `Interval(gt=0)` | `-5` | ValidationError | **accepted** |
| `Interval(gt=0)` | `0` | ValidationError | **accepted** |
| `Interval(le=0)` | `5` | ValidationError | **accepted** |
| `Interval(lt=0)` | `5` | ValidationError | **accepted** |
| `Interval(ge=1, le=10)` | `-5` | ValidationError | ValidationError (control: non-zero bound is fine) |

The non-zero control confirms the trigger is specifically the zero bound, not `Interval` in general. Zero is a very common lower bound, so this silently weakens validation in ordinary usage.

The fix looks like changing the four checks to `if constraint.ge is not None:` (and likewise for `gt`/`le`/`lt`).

This is related to, but distinct from, #13446 - that one is about `Gt` being dropped on a numeric type mismatch, whereas this is the `Interval` branch dropping zero bounds regardless of type.

Happy to open a PR if that would help.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated

import annotated_types
from pydantic import TypeAdapter
from pydantic.experimental.pipeline import validate_as

ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[int, validate_as(int).constrain(annotated_types.Interval(ge=0, le=10))])

print(ta.validate_python(-5))  # -> -5   (expected: ValidationError, ge=0 is violated)
ta.validate_python(20)         # -> ValidationError (le=10 is enforced correctly)

# A non-zero lower bound behaves correctly:
ta2 = TypeAdapter(Annotated[int, validate_as(int).constrain(annotated_types.Interval(ge=1, le=10))])
ta2.validate_python(-5)        # -> ValidationError (correct)
```

title: RootModel.model_dump() typing signature rejects supported serialization arguments

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same change to the `TYPE_CHECKING`-only `RootModel.model_dump()` declaration. Each one widens `context` to `Any | None`, tightens `include`/`exclude` to `IncEx | None`, and adds `fallback` and `polymorphic_serialization` in the same order as `BaseModel`. Correctness on the reported issue is therefore equivalent.

The difference is in the tests and the surrounding changes.

**Patch B** adds regression cases to `tests/typechecking/root_model.py`, as the issue proposes. Its `assert_type` calls cover `context='prefix'`, `fallback=...` and `polymorphic_serialization=True`. Mypy, Pyright and Pyrefly would reject these before the fix and accept them after. That directly tests the symptom the issue reports, which is static type-checker rejection. B also keeps the `Callable` import inside `TYPE_CHECKING`, which is tidy, and leaves the existing explanatory docstring alone.

**Patch A**'s test is a runtime hack. It sets the global `typing.TYPE_CHECKING = True` and re-executes `root_model.py` as a fresh module. That mutates global interpreter state during the test, and it could break if any `TYPE_CHECKING`-only code in the module, such as the metaclass and `dataclass_transform` tricks, does not run cleanly at runtime. It also never runs a type checker, so it does not confirm the calls actually type-check. The test does catch future signature drift, which has some value. But it also asserts exact docstring equality with `BaseModel.model_dump`, which is brittle.

To satisfy that assertion, Patch A replaces the useful explanatory docstring with a copy of the base docstring. The copied docstring wrongly says `Returns: A dictionary representation of the model` for `RootModel`, whose return value is generally not a dict. It moves the real explanation into a comment. That is churn that adds risk and an inaccuracy.

B is the cleaner, better-targeted fix with the more meaningful tests.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

`RootModel` inherits the runtime implementation of `BaseModel.model_dump()`, but defines a separate declaration under `TYPE_CHECKING` to preserve its more precise return type.

That declaration has diverged from the base method:

- `context` is restricted to `dict[str, Any] | None` instead of `Any | None`.
- `fallback` is missing.
- `polymorphic_serialization` is missing.

As a result, Mypy, Pyright, and Pyrefly reject valid calls that succeed at runtime.

All three calls in the example below succeed at runtime.

Mypy currently reports errors equivalent to:

```text
Argument "context" to "model_dump" of "RootModel" has incompatible type "str"
Unexpected keyword argument "fallback" for "model_dump" of "RootModel"
Unexpected keyword argument "polymorphic_serialization" for "model_dump" of "RootModel"
```

Pyright and Pyrefly report the same signature incompatibilities.

## Expected behavior

The type-checking-only `RootModel.model_dump()` declaration should accept the same parameters, annotations, defaults, and ordering as `BaseModel.model_dump()`, while preserving the more precise `RootModel` return annotation.

## Cause

The declaration appears to have drifted as the base method evolved:

- Serialization context originally updated both signatures.
- `BaseModel.context` was later widened to `Any`.
- `fallback` was subsequently added to `BaseModel.model_dump()`.
- `polymorphic_serialization` was later added to `BaseModel.model_dump()`.

Those later changes were not propagated to the manually maintained `RootModel` declaration.

## Proposed fix

Update only the static `RootModel.model_dump()` signature and add focused regression cases to `tests/typechecking/root_model.py`.

No runtime serialization behavior needs to change.

I have prepared and locally validated a focused two-file fix. The following checks pass:

- Mypy type-checking suite
- Pyright type-checking suite
- Pyrefly type-checking suite
- Focused RootModel serialization tests
- Ruff lint and formatting checks
- `git diff --check`

I would be happy to submit the PR after the issue is reviewed and assigned.

### Example Code

```Python
from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, RootModel, SerializationInfo, model_serializer


class ContextRoot(RootModel[str]):
    @model_serializer
    def serialize_root(self, info: SerializationInfo) -> str:
        return f'{info.context}:{self.root}'


class Unknown:
    pass


class Base(BaseModel):
    x: int


class Sub(Base):
    y: int


ContextRoot(root='value').model_dump(context='prefix')

RootModel[Any](root=Unknown()).model_dump(
    mode='json',
    fallback=lambda _: 'fallback',
)

RootModel[list[Base]](root=[Sub(x=1, y=2)]).model_dump(
    polymorphic_serialization=True,
)
```

title: Unexpected serialization schema with `ValidateAs`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the core issue the same way: they give the ValidateAs after-validator a serialization schema built from the annotated (source) type, wrapped in a pass-through wrap serializer. Neither keeps the from_type serializer.

Correctness: B is more careful. It builds the source schema with `handler.generate_schema(source)`, so annotations listed before ValidateAs are not applied a second time; its test checks that JSON-schema examples are not duplicated. It keeps an existing custom serializer such as a preceding PlainSerializer. It skips the wrapper when the source schema equals the inner schema, and it silences ArbitraryTypeWarning while probing. A calls `handler(source)`, which re-runs the earlier annotations and can apply them twice. A also always installs a wrap serializer, even when it is unnecessary.

Scope: B also applies the same fix to pipeline `transform`, which has the identical bug. That is extra scope, but it is coherent, low-risk and tested.

Tests: A's main test only checks `model_dump_json() == '{"x":2}'`. That likely passes even before the fix, because pydantic-core warns and then falls back to inference, so the test does not really catch the regression. B runs its assertions with warnings turned into errors, so its tests fail before the fix and pass after. B also covers the arbitrary-type fallback, a dataclass target, the PlainSerializer case, non-duplication of annotations, and the pipeline cases.

Overall B is the more robust fix with meaningfully better tests.

title: Generic __pydantic_extra__ typevar substitution lost in non-generic subclasses of parametrized models

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the reported case. For `class Sub(M[int])`, when `__pydantic_extra__` is only inherited, each reuses the parent's already-substituted `PydanticExtraInfo`, so `Sub` gets `dict[str, int]`, validates extras, and emits `additionalProperties: {'type': 'integer'}`.

The patches differ at the edges.

**Incomplete parent annotations.** Patch A reuses the parent's extra info even when it is incomplete, and only substitutes when `typevars_map` is non-empty. Take a parent with a forward reference that couldn't be resolved at its own definition time, such as `'dict[str, Later]'` defined in another module. A subclass created after `Later` exists would then inherit an incomplete info instead of re-evaluating the hint. On main today, the hint would be re-evaluated in the declaring class's namespace and resolve correctly. So Patch A risks a regression here, and it imports the #12000-style limitation into a path that currently works. Patch B explicitly falls back to `type_hints['__pydantic_extra__']` when the parent info is incomplete, avoiding this. It also adds a cross-module test for exactly that scenario.

**Choosing the parent.** Patch A takes the first direct base whose `getattr(base, '__pydantic_extra_info__')` is non-None. Patch B walks the MRO to find the class that actually declares the annotation, then takes the most-derived class at or before it that has its own `__pydantic_extra_info__`. This matches how annotation resolution works and is more robust under multiple inheritance and diamonds.

**Tests.** Patch A adds one test covering the basic case. Patch B covers the basic case, a two-level non-generic subclass (`SubSub`), extra-info inherited from a second base, and the cross-module incomplete case. Patch B's tests are broader and target real edge cases.

**Craft.** Patch B's helper adds some code but is well documented. It keeps the existing `replace_types` flow intact instead of branching on `typevars_map`.

Overall, Patch B is more correct at the edges and better tested.

### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2 (`main` @ 428b0dba8)
- [x] I have searched GitHub for a duplicate issue and I'm sure this is something new

### Description

Follow-up to #13369 / #13391 (`__pydantic_extra__` typevar substitution, currently main-only): the substitution works for direct parametrization (`M[int]`) but is lost in a plain (non-generic) subclass of a parametrized model (`class Sub(M[int])`). Extras on the subclass are silently **unvalidated** and the JSON schema loses the extras type.

```
M[int](x='nope')  -> ValidationError (correct, fixed by #13391)
Sub(x='nope')     -> accepted; m.x == 'nope'          # BUG
Sub(x='5').x      -> '5' (str)  vs  M[int](x='5').x == 5

M[int].model_json_schema()['additionalProperties']  -> {'type': 'integer'}
Sub.model_json_schema()['additionalProperties']     -> {}                  # BUG
Sub.__pydantic_extra_info__                          -> PydanticExtraInfo(annotation=dict[str, ~T], complete=True)
```

Root cause (from stepping through `collect_model_fields` in `pydantic/_internal/_fields.py`): for `Sub`, `typevars_map` is empty (its own `__pydantic_generic_metadata__` is empty) and the inherited hint for `__pydantic_extra__` is the parent's *raw* annotation `dict[str, T]` — so `_generics.replace_types(ann, typevars_map)` is a no-op and the raw `~T` survives, producing `extras_schema = {'type': 'any'}`. Regular fields don't have this problem because they're copied from the parent's already-substituted `model_fields`; the extra-info path never consults the parent's `__pydantic_extra_info__` (which on `M[int]` correctly holds `dict[str, int]`).

Note the 2-level generic chain (`class Mid(M[T], Generic[T])`; `Mid[int]`) works on main — only the plain-subclass case is broken.

I have a small fix working locally (reuse the parent's substituted `PydanticExtraInfo` annotation when `__pydantic_extra__` is only inherited, mirroring how fields inherit; brings extra-info to exact parity with fields, including the same known deferred-annotation limitation as #12000), with a regression test in the style of `test_extra_generic_class` — it passes the `test_main.py` / `test_generics.py` / `test_forward_ref.py` / `test_edge_cases.py` suites with no new failures. Per the contributing guidelines I'd like to be assigned before opening the PR — happy to submit it right away.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Generic, TypeVar
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

T = TypeVar('T')

class M(BaseModel, Generic[T]):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra='allow')
    __pydantic_extra__: dict[str, T]
    y: T

class Sub(M[int]):
    pass

print(Sub(y=1, x='not_an_int').x)  # 'not_an_int' — should raise ValidationError
print(Sub.model_json_schema().get('additionalProperties'))  # {} — should be {'type': 'integer'}
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```text

title: Support Ellipsis

judge.reasoning:
Patch A is the more complete fix for the issue's use case, so it wins on correctness, which carries the most weight. Patch B is the more principled core-level design but delivers less of what the issue asks for.

Correctness:
- Patch A registers both `EllipsisType` and the bare `Ellipsis` object as supported annotations. The issue's example literally writes `int | Ellipsis`.
- A gives a full round trip. Python mode accepts only the `...` singleton via `is_instance_schema`. JSON mode accepts the string `'...'` and converts it back to `...`. Serialization emits `'...'` in JSON mode and keeps `...` in Python mode. JSON schema generation works, producing `const '...'`.
- A's serializer raises `PydanticSerializationUnexpectedValue` for non-ellipsis values, so unions where Ellipsis comes first still fall through correctly. A dedicated test checks this.
- Patch B adds a native Rust validator and serializer, but only maps `EllipsisType`. A bare `Ellipsis` annotation, as in the issue, is not handled.
- B's validator rejects every JSON input, because `as_python()` returns None for JSON input. `dump_json` deliberately errors, and JSON schema raises `PydanticInvalidForJsonSchema`.
- So under B, any model with an Ellipsis field cannot be dumped to or loaded from JSON, or produce a schema. For a model field, as in the issue's example, that is a significant usability gap.

Tests:
- A's tests exercise both annotation forms, unions inside tuples, strict mode, Python and JSON dump, JSON validation, round trip, error shapes, union serialization ordering and the JSON schema.
- B's tests cover basic validation and Python dump, and assert that the JSON paths fail.

Scope and craft:
- B touches much more code across Rust and core_schema, with a new error type and serializer, to deliver less functionality.
- A is a small, localized change in `_generate_schema` with docs. Its one wart is the long generated union-member name in error locations.

### Initial Checks

- [x] I have searched Google & GitHub for similar requests and couldn't find anything
- [x] I have read and followed [the docs](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/) and still think this feature is missing

### Description

`Ellipsis` is a builtin type that `pydantic` does not support. Its usage is infrequent, but it can be useful to express placeholders:

This is a bit of a contrived example, but:
```python
class Model(pydantic.BaseModel):
    m: list[list[float]]
    subset: tuple[int | Ellipsis, int | Ellipsis]

    def subset_arr(self) -> np.NDArray:
        return np.asarray(self.m)[*self.subset]
```

Here's how I implement this right now with an adapter: https://github.com/psalvaggio/scientific_pydantic/blob/main/src/scientific_pydantic/ellipsis.py

However, since this is a standard library type, I think this would be a good thing to live in `pydantic` itself.

title: Experimental pipeline: every constraint chained after `ge`/`lt`/`le` is dropped from the JSON schema

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the reported root cause: they stop wrapping the schema in a `function-after` validator once the native `ge`/`lt`/`le`/`multiple_of` field has been set. That lets later constraints in the chain reach the JSON schema. The difference is what happens when the same constraint appears twice.

**Patch A introduces a validation regression.** It writes the native field unconditionally and drops the fallback check, so a repeated constraint overwrites the earlier one. `validate_as(int).ge(5).ge(1)` ends with `ge=1` and accepts 3. `multiple_of(2).multiple_of(3)` ends with `multiple_of=3` and accepts 3. Before the patch, the earlier bound survived inside the function wrapper, so validation was correct; Patch A breaks that. The issue specifically stresses that validation is currently correct, so this is a real step backward.

Patch A also removes the type-match guards (int bound on int schema, float on float, Decimal on decimal). It relies on its own comment that pydantic-core will cast a mismatched bound, such as `gt=1.5` on an int schema. That is unverified and riskier than keeping the guarded fallback. It does add tests for mixed-type bounds and the chain cases from the issue, but nothing for repeated constraints.

**Patch B avoids that regression.** It follows the `native_constraint_applied` shape the issue proposes, consistently across Gt/Ge/Lt/Le/MultipleOf. It keeps the type-match guards, so mismatched bounds still go through the fallback validator. When a bound is repeated it merges them, keeping the stricter value via `max`/`min`. For a second `multiple_of`, which can't be merged, it keeps the first native and adds a function check for the second.

Patch B also extends the same treatment to `Len` and adjusts `str_strip` so a length check placed before stripping still sees the unstripped value. That goes beyond the issue, but it is coherent, needed for the `Len` change to be correct, and tested.

Patch B's tests check both the JSON schema and validation for every scenario in the issue, plus float and Decimal variants. They also cover repeated constraints keeping the strictest bound, len-then-strip ordering, and the Gt fallback on a type mismatch.

On correctness, which is the most important criterion, Patch B is clearly better.

issue_md:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

In the experimental pipeline API, chaining constraints silently drops every bound after the first from the generated JSON schema. **Validation stays correct** - only the published schema is wrong, which makes it easy to miss.

All bounds below are non-zero, so this is not #13450 (falsy zero bounds in `Interval`). Observed identically on released 2.13.4 and on `main` (2.14.0a1).

| expression | JSON schema | validation |
|---|---|---|
| `validate_as(int).ge(1).le(100)` | `{"minimum": 1, "type": "integer"}` | 0 reject, 50 accept, 200 reject |
| `validate_as(int).le(100).ge(1)` | `{"maximum": 100, "type": "integer"}` | 0 reject, 50 accept, 200 reject |
| `validate_as(int).constrain(Interval(ge=1, le=100))` | `{"minimum": 1, "type": "integer"}` | 0 reject, 50 accept, 200 reject |
| `validate_as(int).ge(1).le(100).multiple_of(5)` | `{"minimum": 1, "type": "integer"}` | correct |
| `validate_as(int).gt(1).lt(100)` *(control)* | `{"exclusiveMinimum": 1, "exclusiveMaximum": 100, ...}` | correct |
| `Annotated[int, Ge(1), Le(100)]` *(control)* | `{"minimum": 1, "maximum": 100, ...}` | correct |

So `.ge(1).le(100).multiple_of(5)` publishes a schema advertising *any integer >= 1*, while the validator rejects 200 and 52. For FastAPI that means the OpenAPI component and every generated client disagree with the server.

### Cause

In `_apply_constraint()`, the `Ge`, `Lt` and `Le` branches apply their fallback function validator **unconditionally** - including when the native core-schema field was just set:

```python
elif isinstance(constraint, annotated_types.Ge):
    ge = constraint.ge
    if s and s['type'] in {'int', 'float', 'decimal'}:
        s = s.copy()
        if s['type'] == 'int' and isinstance(ge, int):
            s['ge'] = ge          # native constraint applied...
        ...

    def check_ge(v: Any) -> bool:
        return v >= ge

    s = _check_func(check_ge, f'>= {ge}', s)   # ...and then wrapped anyway
```

`_check_func` wraps the schema in `function-after`. The next constraint in the chain sees `s['type'] == 'function-after'`, which is not in `{'int', 'float', 'decimal'}`, so it cannot set its own native field and survives only inside an opaque callable that JSON-schema generation cannot read. Core schema for `.ge(1).le(100)`:

```
{'type': 'function-after',
 'function': ...,                       # <- le(100) lives in here, invisible to the schema
 'schema': {'type': 'function-after',
            'function': ...,            # <- redundant ge check
            'schema': {'type': 'int', 'ge': 1}}}
```

`Gt` is the control that works, and only by accident: its fallback sits in an `else:`, so nothing is wrapped when the native constraint applies.

### Relationship to the open PRs in this function

Two in-flight PRs each fix one branch of this, for unrelated reasons, and between them they leave `Ge`, `Lt` and `Le` untouched:

- **#13473** adds a `native_constraint_applied` flag to `MultipleOf` to avoid a float parity problem. Same shape as the fix needed here.
- **#13446** restructures `Gt` so the fallback lands inside the numeric branch.

Worth flagging on the second one: #13446's description argues that `Gt` is *uniquely* broken and holds up `Ge`/`Lt`/`Le`/`MultipleOf` as the correct model, because they "always apply" the check and so enforce the bound on a type mismatch. That is true of validation, but always applying it is exactly what destroys the schema. `Gt` is uniquely broken for validation; the other four are broken for schema. Whichever way this is fixed, it probably wants to be one symmetric change across all five branches rather than three separate patches.

### Example Code

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import TypeAdapter
from pydantic.experimental.pipeline import validate_as

ta = TypeAdapter(Annotated[int, validate_as(int).ge(1).le(100)])

print(ta.json_schema())      # {'minimum': 1, 'type': 'integer'}   <- no maximum
ta.validate_python(200)      # ValidationError, as it should be

# control: the same constraints without the pipeline
import annotated_types
print(TypeAdapter(Annotated[int, annotated_types.Ge(1), annotated_types.Le(100)]).json_schema())
# {'maximum': 100, 'minimum': 1, 'type': 'integer'}
```

### Python, Pydantic & OS Version

```text
             pydantic version: 2.13.4
        pydantic-core version: 2.46.4
          pydantic-core build: profile=release pgo=false
               python version: 3.11.15 (main, Mar  3 2026, 09:26:23) [GCC 13.3.0]
                     platform: Linux-6.18.5-x86_64-with-glibc2.39
             related packages: typing_extensions-4.16.0
                       commit: unknown
```

I have a PR ready that applies the `native_constraint_applied` shape from #13473 to `Ge`/`Lt`/`Le`, with regression tests that fail without it. Happy to open it, or to fold it into one of the existing PRs if you'd rather land a single change.

title: Generic model parametrization drops field defaults and typevar substitution after `__annotations__` is read on a metaclass (Python <= 3.13)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same root-cause fix. On Python <= 3.13, when `obj` is a class, `safe_get_annotations` reads own annotations from `obj.__dict__` instead of using `getattr`. This avoids the inherited-annotations leak that happens when a metaclass's `__dict__` holds a plain `__annotations__` dict shadowing the `type.__annotations__` descriptor. The issue suggests exactly this approach, so on correctness of the core fix they are essentially equal.

Patch A adds one extra guard. If the `__dict__` entry is a `GetSetDescriptorType` (the case where `obj` is `type` itself), it returns `{}` rather than the descriptor object. It also documents the rationale in the docstring. This edge case is unlikely in practice, but it makes the function robust for any class input.

On tests, Patch A is clearly stronger:
- Its generic test reproduces the reported scenario end-to-end. It defines a custom `ModelMetaclass` subclass, reads its `__annotations__`, and parametrizes `G[str]`. It then checks that defaults are kept, the typevar is substituted, invalid input is rejected, and generic and non-generic subclasses still work. This would fail before the fix.
- It also adds a pydantic dataclass inheritance test, confirming that parent fields keep their parent-namespace evaluation and `FieldInfo` metadata under the same poisoning.

Patch B adds only a direct unit test of `safe_get_annotations` on a plain-metaclass hierarchy. That test is valid and would fail before the fix, but it does not exercise the user-visible symptom (dropped defaults and missing typevar substitution in generic parametrization).

Scope is comparable and minimal in both. Patch A wins on test coverage of the actual reported behavior and slightly better edge-case handling and documentation.
